(p-369) Surah Ibrahim (peace be upon him)

"In the name of Allah" — the One who is singular in perfection, and exalted above having any equal or likeness. "The Most Gracious" to all His creation with a Book that is the ultimate in clarity. "The Most Merciful" who chose from among His servants those whom He bound to the spirit of His love. ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾ The aim of the surah is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and an explanation that this Book is the ultimate conveyance to Allah, because it is responsible for clarifying the path that indicates Him and leads to Him. It transports people, with the secrets it contains, from one state to another, as the letter ra' indicates. The most evident example of this purpose is the story of Ibrahim, peace and blessings be upon him. As for tawhid, it is clear. As for the matter of the Book, it is because it is among the content of his supplication for his offspring, those whom he settled near the Sacred House from the descendants of Isma'il, peace be upon him: ﴿"Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129].

When He concluded al-Ra'd by stating that no testimony equals the testimony from Him, "knowledge of the Book" is an indication that the Book itself is the witness to its own inimitability, through its eloquence and through what it contains of (p-370) the various fields of knowledge. He brought it in that context, defining what was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah and elsewhere. Then its description was repeated in [Surahs Yunus, Hud, Yusuf and al-Ra'd] as wise, firmly structured, detailed, and clarifying, and that it is the truth that is established, such that the firm mountains may vanish while it remains steadfast, not wavering in any part and no meaning of it being shaken. He mentioned it at the beginning of [this] surah in an indefinite form of magnification, saying: ﴿A Book﴾, meaning a great Book in degrees of greatness that your intellects cannot bear to describe by any other attribute. The explanation of its description as "clear" indicates that it is in Arabic, and the implied meaning is: ﴿We have sent it down﴾, meaning by Our majesty, "to you" in the tongue of your people, so that you may make it clear to them.

When the description combined the attributes that necessitate success, mentioned at the beginning of the surah and supported by every shining proof and manifest authority, it became such that whoever comprehends the realities of those qualities does not hesitate to gather its fruit. After detailing what is at the beginning of al-Baqarah in the preceding surah, as has passed, He stirred desire for that fruit with what urges toward it and draws the heart of every intelligent person to it, saying: ﴿To bring forth mankind﴾, meaning the common people of your nation and others, through your calling them to it, even if they are in disorder, ﴿from the darknesses﴾, which are many kinds of misguidance produced by ignorance, ﴿into the light﴾, which is one, and it is the path of Allah, the guidance to which is called for in al-Fatihah. Or, "to make clear to the Arabs, your people," because it is in their tongue, a healing clarification, so that you make them — by the compelling proofs you establish upon them, the clear arguments you explain to them, the manifest signs you set up for them, and the overwhelming evidences you ordain for them — as in the light of day, by what He has opened of their locked sights and uncovered from the coverings of their hearts, so that they are able to come out of the darknesses of disbelief, which are the ways of Satan, into the light of faith, which is His path: ﴿And do not follow the paths, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. He likened faith and what guides to it to light, because it is the protection of the intellect from error on the road to Allah, just as light is the protection of sight from straying from the sensory path. When they come out into the light, they are worthy of bringing all people out ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, meaning the Benefactor to them. The "permission" (idhn) is the release to act by a saying heard by the ear; this is its root, as stated by al-Rummani.

When the light was general, He explained it by way of resumption or apposition, by repeating the governing particle, saying: ﴿To the path of the Mighty﴾, who is exalted above attributes of deficiency (p-372), so that no one may enter His path, which is His Lord, or approach its traveler without His permission, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, who encompasses all perfection, so He alone deserves all praise by His essence and by the bounties He pours out upon His servants, through which He nurtures them and is praised by them in every state. How much more so when they follow His path, which is clear, broad and easy!

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 2:

When he (Allah) attributed the path of salvation to two descriptions, each of which may be applied to creation, he separated them with His noble proper name, "Allah" (Allāh), as a fresh sentence (isti'nāf) in the reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, where it is in the nominative (raf'). And in the reading of the rest, where it is in the genitive (jarr), it is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān), because it functions as a proper noun (ism 'alam), being specific to the One worshipped in truth. He described Him with what His oneness requires, so He said: "Allah," that is, the One who encompasses by knowledge and power, ﴿the One to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, that is, the high bodies, from the spheres and others. Since the context concerns indicating the Creator and affirming His oneness, He emphasized by repeating the relative pronoun together with its relative clause, and said: ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾, that is: woe to whoever associates anything with Him from them or in them, for it is clearest that what is owned cannot be a partner.

It is also possible that the sense is: "Then there is a woe (waʾl), and salvation and safety, for whoever is guided by it and comes out of the darkness of disbelief." "Woe" (wayl) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning destruction (halāk); it is put in the accusative as verbal nouns are, and then put in the nominative (rafʿ) to indicate that the meaning of destruction, which is the opposite of waʾl, the salvation, is established ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, those who concealed the proofs of their intellects, ﴿from a severe punishment﴾ whose pains and intensity multiply. And severity (shiddah) is a gathering in which separation is hard.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 3:

When he had indicated what awaits the disbelievers, he described them by that which prevents them from accepting good and leaves them in the valleys of evil, saying: ﴿Those who prefer the worldly life﴾ — that is, they seek to love it or to find love for it with the utmost desire, following their whims (hawa) — ﴿the life of this world﴾, which is the first creation, the abode of transit, preferring it ﴿over the Hereafter﴾, that is, the other creation, which is the abode of permanence. This is by their following their own souls in loving it, until they are as if they were seeking that. This is evidence that love may come through volition. Love (al-mahabbah) is the inclination of natures toward a thing through desire. They refrain, fearing for their worldly affairs, of which their leadership is part, from following the path. ("And") they add to that that they "bar" (yasuddun), that is, they turn away themselves and prevent others ﴿from the way of God﴾, that is, the road of the Supreme King; and the sabil (way) is the course prepared for travel. ("And") they go further in that they "seek it" (yabghunaha), that is, they seek for it, the preposition being omitted and the verb made to reach its object for emphasis ﴿crookedness﴾. And 'iwaj (crookedness) is a deviation from straightness; it is with a kasra on the 'ayn in matters of religion, affairs and land, and with a fatha in everything that is upright, like a wall, a spear and the like. ﴿Those﴾, that is, the remote, the hateful ones, ﴿are in far error﴾, that is, far from the truth. This is a metaphorical attribution, because it is the far-off ones who are in error, by their inclination from the enduring to the perishing, and by their seeking crookedness in that which God, who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, has made straight.

When he had mentioned [what is understood] that He sent him ﷺ in the tongue of his people to mankind generally, because the Arabic tongue is the easiest, most comprehensive, most eloquent and clearest of tongues, and thus it was of the utmost justice, and concluded that the path to Him is of the utmost uprightness and moderation, this indicated the nobility of this tongue, for its suitability for all nations and its ease for them, in contrast to the tongue of each of the Messengers being specific to his own people. Therefore He followed it with His saying: ﴿And We did not send﴾, that is, by what We have of majesty, and He intensified the negation by saying: ﴿any messenger﴾, that is, at any time among the times, ﴿except in the tongue﴾, that is, the language of ''his people'', that is, those among whom there is the capacity to strive to understand what they wish, ''so that he might make clear'', that is, a sufficient clarification ﴿to them﴾, as was previously stated: "We have sent you with an Arabic Book, in the tongue of your people, so that you may make [it] clear to them" (p-375) and to all of creation. Indeed your tongue is the easiest and sweetest of tongues. So it is coordinated with ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], according to the interpretation previously mentioned. When this is established, it becomes known that there is then no barrier for any nation among the nations to remaining upright upon this path, except by the permission of Allah and His will. ﴿So He leads astray﴾, that is, as a consequence of that, He leads astray ''Allah'', that is, the One to whom all command belongs, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to be led astray. He, glorified is He, placed this first out of concern to show that He, glorified is He, is the Creator of evil just as He is the Creator of good, even though the context is a censure of the disbelievers, who are the leaders of the people of misguidance. ﴿And He guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance, for He, glorified is He, is the One who misguides and the One who guides. As for the Messengers, they are clarifiers who establish the proof, to distinguish the one who is astray from the one who is guided. ﴿''And He''﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿''the Mighty''﴾, the One whose what is with Him cannot be attained except through Him, and nothing He wills is prevented from Him, ﴿the Wise﴾, the One whose designing is not undone. Therefore, by His wisdom He arranged the sending of His messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to creation generally in the Arabic tongue, because the intent is to gather creation upon the truth. So He gathered them upon one tongue, which is most fitting for that. Had it been sent down in all tongues, it would have contradicted this intent. Even if it were accompanied by miraculousness in every tongue, it would have been close to compulsion, and faith in the unseen would be lost. It would also lead to the claim of the people of every tongue (p-376) that expressing [it] in their tongue is greater, which would lead to boasting and partisanship, which leads to the most severe division. The most suitable tongue is the tongue of the people of the Messenger, because they are closest to him. Thus their understanding of the secrets of his law and their comprehension of its realities would be easier, and they would be farthest from error and mistake. When they understood from him, they would call those who come after them to translation [tarajim, i.e., translators] and so on. Thus the matter would spread, become general, and be facilitated, and it would, along with that, be farther from distortion and safer from dispute.

Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: When [Surat al-Ra'd] was upon what paves the way, in that those signs and proofs that preceded it leave no doubt for one who reflects upon them, to magnify their affair and clarify their matter, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], that is, if they remember by it, become insightful through its proofs, and reflect upon its signs. ﴿And if only a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved or the earth were cleft asunder﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. Since this guidance and misguidance are all contingent upon His will, glorified is He, and His prior decree, and He had said to His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], He, exalted is He, said here: ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], meaning: upon you is only the conveying. When He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yusuf: 105], its exposition was completed (p-377) in [Surat al-Ra'd]. Here He informed that all of that belongs to Him and to His dominion, so He said: ﴿to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 2]. Thus the heavens and the earth in their totality, and whatever is in them of great things by which the lesson has been made clear to you, all of that belongs to Him in dominion, creation, and origination.

﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [Al 'Imran: 83]. ﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 2], because of their obstinacy despite the clarity and explicitness of the matter. ﴿Who hinder [others] from the way of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 3], despite the clarity of the way and the adoption of that guidance. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the tongue of his people﴾. It seems that this is part of His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]. That is because the disbelievers, when envy and obstinacy carried them away, and understanding was far from what was innately disposed in their hearts and sealed upon them, denied that the Messengers could be from among humans, until they said: ﴿Is it a human who guides us?﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6], ﴿You are not but human like us﴾ [Ya-Sin: 15]. And Quraysh said: ﴿Why was an angel not sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8], ﴿What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of the two cities, great?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. This did not increase among them, and their successors followed their predecessors in it. He, exalted is He, refuted their leaders and nullified their delusion in verses that came down gradually (p-378) regarding this purpose, little by little. The first of what came in that regard, in the context of refuting them, and in the order of the surahs of the Book, is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them?﴾ [Yunus: 2], the verse. Then He followed that with His singular act of creation, origination, management, and lordship. And within that is that He does what He wills, because all of it is His creation and His dominion, and that He is the All-Knowing of the wisdom in sending the messengers and their being human. Thus Allah, exalted is He, humbled through the content of these verses every obstinate denier. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned in [Surat Hud] the saying of the people of Noah: ﴿We do not see you but as a human like us﴾ [Hud: 27], the verse, and his answer, peace be upon him: ﴿Have you considered, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, but it has been concealed from you? Shall we compel you to it while you are averse to it?﴾ [Hud: 28], meaning: although I am, in humanity, like you, Allah has specially favored me with His grace, given me mercy from Himself, and given me a proof for what I brought to you from Him. In this story is the greatest admonition. Then this occurred with Salih and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both. The habit of nations always with their prophets is the commission of these statements, and in them is deviation and inability to contend with them, which is not hidden, and which is evidence of their obstinacy. Then He, glorified is He, increased [exalted is He] (p-379) His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, in acquainting him with the circumstances of those Prophets who preceded him, peace be upon them, so that whoever experiences what they experienced would hear of it, and so He said the same as their statement. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]. He informed that this does not diminish any of their ranks; rather it occurs in the establishment of the proof upon the servants. Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the tongue of his people﴾, that is, so that it would be more eloquent in the proof and more decisive in removing excuse. For they might say, when the languages differ: "We do not understand them," since they said that even when the languages agree. The people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said: ﴿We do not understand much of what you say﴾ [Hud: 91], and he, peace be upon him, was addressing them in their own tongue. So how much more so if it were otherwise! Indeed, if the Messengers, peace be upon them, differed from their nations in abstaining from marriage and not taking wives and children, and in the use of foods and other familiar things of humans, it would have been repellent. Thus the wisdom in their being human has become clear. [Had they been of the angels, aversion and flight would have occurred due to the difference in kind, and to this refers His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them as they are confusing﴾ [al-An'am: 9], that is, so that he would be closer to them, lest aversion occur. Thus their being human is closer and more upright for the proof.] And since the mission of Muhammad ﷺ was general, he (p-380) peace be upon him, would address each group among the groups of the Arabs in its own tongue and speak to it in what it understands. Consider how much difference there is between his letter, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning charity, and his letter to Wa'il ibn Hujr, despite the unity of purpose. There are parallels to these two letters which one may find in their proper places. All of this is so that the proof may be established upon everyone. The remainder of [Surat Ibrahim], peace be upon him, continued in acquainting [the reader] with the condition of those who deny the messengers, the threat against those who oppose them, and the explanation of some of the terrors of the Hereafter and its punishment. End.

When Glorified is He had mentioned the Messengers with what He mentioned, the listener anticipated a detailed account of some of their news. So He began with a mention from His Book, the most noble book after the Qur'an, as "guidance for mankind," as evidence that He does what He wills of misguidance and guidance, as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), as firm support and patience against the harm of his people, and as guidance toward what is good for them in addressing them. He said, introducing it with the particle of anticipation: ﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾, i.e., with Our greatness; ﴿with Our signs﴾, i.e., the clear proofs. Then He explained the sending with His words: ﴿"Bring your people out﴾, i.e., those among whom there is strength to overcome affairs (p-381) ﴿from the darknesses﴾, i.e., kinds of ignorance, ﴿into the light﴾ through those signs; ﴿and remind them﴾, i.e., a great reminding, ﴿of the Days of Allah﴾, i.e., of Him to whom belong majesty and honour, from His events among the earlier nations and other than that, of the bestowals upon His friends and the trials of His enemies, just as We sent you for that purpose." ﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in that great reminding, ﴿are signs﴾ of the oneness of Allah and His greatness ﴿for everyone who is patient, grateful.﴾ i.e., one who is exceedingly patient under the trial of Allah. He said in al-Awarif: Abu al-Hasan ibn Salim said: they are three: the one who feigns patience (mutasabbir), the patient one (sabir), and the one who is very patient (sabbar). The mutasabbir is the one who is patient for Allah; sometimes he is patient and sometimes he panics. The sabir is the one who is patient for Allah [and for Allah] and does not panic, but he anticipates complaint from himself, and panic may at times overpower him. As for the sabbar, he is the one whom Allah has made patient for Allah, by Allah, and through Allah. Such a person, even if all afflictions befall him, does not panic or change, in terms of obligation and reality, not in terms of outward form (p-382) and creation. His allusion in this is the manifestation of the judgment of knowledge in him together with the manifestation of the attribute of nature.

﴿grateful﴾, i.e., greatly thankful for His blessings, for His days with His friends are never free of either a blessing or a affliction. The intensive form (of the word) points to the fact that His custom, exalted is He, is that He only grants victory to His friends after a long testing with great affliction, so that the truthful may be distinguished from the liar: ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him say, "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]; ﴿until, when the Messengers despaired﴾ [Yusuf: 110]; ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1]; ﴿Do people think they will be left [to say, "We believe"] and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. This is because nothing is harder on souls than parting from what is familiar, especially if it is a religion, and especially if the ancestors had followed it. Hence no one stands up to call to the religion except one who has reached the peak of patience.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 6:

When He mentioned what Musa (peace be upon him) was commanded, and His command to the Noble One (ﷺ) had already preceded, to follow the Prophets, who are the leaders among them and the possessors of firm resolve, it was as if it were said: "So make clear to the people what was sent down to them, and remind them of the Days of Allah, following the example of your brother Musa (peace be upon him), and mention to them his account, for his days are among the greatest of the Days of Allah: the hardest of trials and the most magnificent of bounties." ﴿And when Musa said﴾, complying with what We commanded him, ﴿to his people﴾, reminding them of the Days of Allah among them, then His Days with others.

Since the purpose of reminding them of the Days is to increase encouragement and warning, He indicated that the station of warning here is more important, to urge them to abandon their error. He left out the tender address of compassion used in [al-Baqara and al-Ma'ida], such as the words "O my people" (ﷺ-style softness), by omitting it here, to indicate that the situation requires conveying the message concisely, out of fear that they would be hastened into punishment. So He said: ﴿Remember the favour of Allah﴾, that is, of the Lord of Majesty and Honour. He expressed by "favour" the bestowal, to urge reasoning from the effect to the one who causes it: ﴿upon you﴾. Then He substituted for "favour" the phrase "when," which is an adverbial of the favour.

Since they had endured for a very long time through the length of their affliction at the hands of Pharaoh, in a manner by which, in the usual course, their deliverance from him was impossible, and even if it were possible at a distance, it would only have come after very long periods and with severe exhaustion, He indicated the swiftness of their deliverance by comparison with Him, had it proceeded according to the usual course, as a reward for their long patience. So He used the form (anjā) rather than the intensive form (najjā) that the context of al-Baqara required, and He said: ﴿He delivered you from﴾ the affliction of ﴿the folk of Pharaoh﴾, that is, Pharaoh himself and his followers, using the shared term in both of its meanings, since "āl" applies to the person himself and to a man's family and followers and allies. Al-Qamus says: "It is not used except for what has nobility, generally." So it was as if they said: "From which of their afflictions?" He said: ﴿who inflicted upon you﴾, that is, who imposed upon you and put you in charge in a manner of contempt and subjugation, ﴿the terrible torment﴾ through enslavement.

Since the context concerns eloquent patience, that required the conjunction in His words: ﴿and they slaughtered﴾, that is, slaughtering many and causing death, by what the expression "killing" in al-A'raf conveys, and by the repetition of the expression "slaughtering," specifying that death by the knife is meant, ﴿your sons, and let live﴾, that is, sought to keep alive, ﴿your women﴾, to indicate that this is another affliction. And the situation is that ﴿in that﴾ [Ibrahim: 6; cf. al-An'am: 99], that is, the matter of great hardship from the [previously mentioned] torment or the deliverance, or both, ﴿is a great trial from your Lord﴾, that is, the Nurturer of you, the Manager of your affairs.

And when He reminded them of the blessing of security, He encouraged them toward what increases it and warned them against what removes it, so He said: "And when" — i.e., remember when ﴿your Lord proclaimed⦆ — i.e., He made it known to you, the One who did good to you, with an eloquent announcement that leaves no room for doubt, saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you⦆. He emphasized it because of the disbelief that people have of the like of this, since they believe that increase comes through striving for provision and decrease through negligence in it, ﴿I will surely increase you⦆ in My blessings, for gratitude is the binder of what exists and the snare of what is lost. "Indeed My bounty is ready, so hope for it" (p-385). ﴿But if you are ungrateful⦆ for the blessing, by not binding it with gratitude, ﴿I will surely take away from you⦆ and ﴿I will surely punish you⦆, ﴿indeed My punishment⦆ by removing it and otherwise ﴿is severe⦆, so fear Him. Thus the verse, as you see, is of the type of *ihtibak* (the rhetorical device of omitting from each half what is mentioned in the other).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 8:

Since whoever urges something and rewards for it, or forbids something and punishes for doing it, does so for a purpose that serves him, he (al-Biqa'i) clarified that Allah, glorified is He, is exalted above having harm or benefit reach Him, and that the harm and benefit of that belong only to the servant. So He, exalted, said, relating from him: ﴿And Moses said﴾, warning them and teaching that the burden of ingratitude (kufran) belongs only to its bearer: ﴿If you disbelieve﴾. Kufr (disbelief) is the squandering of the right of a blessing by denying it, or what takes its place in the bone (i.e., what is equivalent to it in effect). ﴿You and whoever is on the earth﴾, and He emphasized it with His saying "all together," so its harm falls on you specifically, without any of it returning to Allah. ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿is free of need﴾, that is, in His essence and attributes, independent of every single one. The freedom from need here is specific to what negates the reaching of harm or deficiency, and specific to His being capable, whom nothing can overpower, knowing, from whom nothing is hidden, and this is by His own essence, not by anything other than Him. Whoever is not like this is not free of need. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, that is, He deserves praise to the utmost degree because of the great blessings He has and because of the attributes of perfection that belong to Him. Every creature praises Him by its existence, its actions, and all its words, whatever they may be, because His bringing them into existence speaks of His praise, glorified is He.

(p-٣٨٦)

He mentions the proclamation of that which is recalled from the Torah:

He said in the Fifth Book: "The Lord your God has chosen you to be for Him a beloved people from among all the peoples [who are on the face of the earth, and not because you are more numerous than all the peoples]. The Lord loved you and chose you, but in order to fulfil the oath which He swore to your fathers. Therefore the Lord brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you from bondage, and delivered you from the hand of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that you may know that the Lord your God is the God of truth, a God who watches over, who keeps the blessing and the covenant for His friends who keep His commandment for a thousand generations, and who repays those who hate Him during their lives and recompenses them with destruction and perdition. Keep the statutes, the judgments, and the commandments which I command you today, and do them. The Lord God will keep the covenant and the blessing which He swore to your fathers, and He will love you, bless you, and multiply you, and bless the offspring of your womb, the fruit of your land, your grain, your wine, your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flocks, and you shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall be no barren male or female among you, nor [among] your livestock. The Lord will turn away from you every sickness, and all the plagues of Egypt which Allah sent upon the people of Egypt, as you know, He will not send upon you, but will send them upon all your enemies. You shall eat all the good things of the peoples which the Lord your God gives you, and your eyes shall not pity them, and you shall not serve their gods, for they are a snare to you. And if you say in your hearts: 'These peoples are more than we are, how can we dispossess them?' do not be afraid of them, but remember all that the Lord your God did to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and all his servants, and the great trials which your eyes saw, and the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and the outstretched arm, and how the Lord your God brought you out! Thus will the Lord your God do to all the peoples whom you fear.

And the Lord your God will send against them afflictions until He destroys them, and those who remain and hide from you, do not fear them, for the Lord your God is among you, the great and awesome God. The Lord your God will destroy these peoples from before you little by little, because you cannot destroy them quickly, lest the wild beasts multiply. But (p-٣٨٨) the Lord your God will deliver them up to you, and you shall strike them with a severe blow until you destroy them, and He will deliver their kings into your hands, and you shall destroy their names from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand before you until you destroy them, and you shall burn their graven gods with fire. Do not covet the silver and gold that is on them and take it from them, lest you become defiled by it, for it is an abomination to the Lord your God. So do not bring an abomination into your houses, lest you become accursed like it, but loathe it, defile it, and treat it as an accursed refuse, because it is forbidden. Then [he said]: Behold, I set before you a blessing and a curse. The blessing, you will attain it if you keep the commandments of [Allah] your Lord, and the curse will overtake you if you do not hear the commandments of Allah your Lord, and turn aside from the way which He commanded you today." Many similar things have passed from the Torah. There is no doubt that this encouragement, warning, and reminder for caution, just as it was addressed to the Children of Israel, is for everyone among the obligated who hears it.

[p. 389] When He warned them of God's retribution should they disbelieve, He reminded them of His days among the earlier nations, and He singled out the first three, because they were the strongest in bodies, the most numerous in helpers, the most powerful in their remnants, and the longest-lived. This is because the force of seizure is more terrifying when it becomes manifest in existence, since the soul is more receptive to what is perceived by the senses. [Then He said], indicating what He guided them to, namely His self-sufficiency and His praiseworthiness, and warning them of God's mighty seizures: ﴿Has there not come to you﴾, that is, O Children of Israel, ﴿the news of those﴾. Since the intended people were a specific group and did not encompass all time, He said: ﴿before you﴾. Then He substituted for them, saying: "a people", that is, the news of the people of ﴿Noah﴾, who filled the earth; and "of" the news of "'Ad", who were the strongest of people in body and the firmest of hearts; and "of" the news of "Thamud", who were the most capable of people in hewing rocks and building palaces; and "of" the news of ﴿those﴾. Since the intended here were some, He introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿after them﴾, that is, in time, while they were so numerous that ﴿none knows them﴾, that is, with true knowledge in detail, ﴿except God﴾, that is, He to whom belongs complete encompassment. They disbelieved, so God destroyed them, and He remained Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy at their seizure and at their distance, as He was before them. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say when he recited this verse: "The genealogists have lied." Then He, glory be to Him, explained the matter in detail, saying, in answer to one who seemed to ask: what was their news? ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾. He omitted the conjunction because of the strong connection with the one inquiring about it. ﴿Then they put their hands to their mouths﴾, that is, the nations, immediately upon the coming of the messengers, without reflection, combining in their denial both action and speech. This is an indication of silence about that and of silencing (the messengers), as if it were not fitting for them to utter anything, even by way of rejection. Al-Razi said in Al-Lawami': Abu Ubayd related: "I spoke to him about my need, and he put his hand in his mouth," meaning that he kept silent and did not respond. And, after they did this for these corrupt purposes, ﴿they said﴾, that is, the nations: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which﴾ — that is, we have covered over the vision of our intellects, scorning — and since rejecting the message comprises disbelief, and they did not accept that the one who sent them was God, they used the passive in their statement: ﴿you have been sent with it﴾, [that is] because you have not brought us anything that would necessitate even conjecture, let alone certainty; therefore its rejection does not require reflection.

Since what the messengers brought necessitates certainty by what everyone knows, and since they were, in what they said, open to the charge of denial, they emphasized: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt﴾, that is, encompassing us, which is standing between two opposites without preferring either, alternating in the state of recollection, and contrary to knowledge and ignorance.

Since the call was attributed to the group of messengers, they retained the nun of the nominative with the pronoun of the speakers, unlike what preceded in Hud. So they said: ﴿concerning what﴾, that is, what matter, ﴿you call us﴾, O messengers, ﴿to﴾, that is, of the religion, ﴿disquieting﴾, that is, causing suspicion and falling into doubt, agitation and alarm; from "arabar-rajulu" meaning he became one with suspicion, that is, unease and instability.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 10:

Since the hearer of this statement is eager to learn its answer, and since the call in every religion is rooted in tawhid (the oneness of God), and whoever doubts it is doubting God, and since the matter of God is so evident that no sensible person doubts it when he judges with his intellect free of desire, the denial and the presentation of the statement were permissible on the assumption of an unrestricted, unspecified question in His saying: ﴿their messengers said﴾. Since what they doubted was so evident that no doubt could reach it, they denied that there could be any doubt about it, because that implies a denial of their own doubt and the doubt of others. So they said: ﴿Is there doubt about God﴾, i.e., the One who possesses all attributes of perfection, ﴿doubt﴾.

Since the answer was general and did not single out some people over others, they did not add a qualifier (p-٣٩٢), unlike His saying: ﴿We are only human beings like you﴾ [Ibrahim: 11]. Then they alerted them, through the created order, to the aim of the call: the existence of the Creator, His singularity and His manifestness, in their saying: ﴿the Originator of the heavens﴾. Since the situation called for asserting that this is in the utmost clarity, there was no need for emphasis by repeating the governing verb, so He said: ﴿and the earth﴾, i.e., upon this wondrous pattern and strange design, orderly in its conditions, beautiful in its benefits, and harmonious in its seasons. When they had made the proofs of His oneness clear to them, they explained to them that the fruit of the call is specifically for them, and that no one with even minimal insight would reject it. So they said: ﴿He calls you﴾, i.e., through our tongues, ﴿to forgive you﴾.

Since the unbeliever is first called only to faith, and since faith erases only the sins that preceded it between him and his Lord, not the wrongs done to people, He said: ﴿of your sins﴾. Had the forgiveness been general, it would have implied that after faith they would not be called to any action at all. Nor would they be treated as kings are known to treat those who oppose them, by swift destruction, but rather ﴿He defers you﴾, even if you have erred or intended and then repented, ﴿to a specified term﴾ known to Him through His foreknowledge, which is your appointed times, distributed as they are. He will not uproot you with punishment in a single instant as He did with the nations mentioned.

When He had clarified for them the principal matter with its proof, and then drew out from it what is beyond doubt concerning the restriction of its benefit to them, they knew that they had no answer to it. So they turned away from it and, in obstinacy, said: ﴿You are only﴾, i.e., you, O messengers, are ﴿only human beings﴾, and they emphasized what they intended by negating any distinction, saying: ﴿like us﴾. They meant: what is the reason for your being singled out for prophethood rather than us? Then it was as if it were said: "So what?" They said: ﴿You wish to turn us away﴾, i.e., to divert and deflect us, ﴿from what our fathers worshipped﴾, i.e., a custom that has become like an innate nature. They emphasized this meaning, to remind them of the past state, by using the present tense, saying: ﴿our fathers worshipped﴾. That is, because you are human beings among whom envy occurs, you envied us for following the fathers and intended to abandon us so that we would become your followers. ﴿So bring us﴾, i.e., as a consequence of our not seeing any superiority in you, and our showing that what you intend is an impediment, let us say to you: "Bring us ﴿a manifest authority﴾", i.e., a clear proof that compels us to affirm what you propose to us. This is pure obstinacy, for they deserve to turn away from every authority they bring, whatever it may be, just as they discarded the clear signs that they had brought, and so they did not count them (p-٣٩٤).

So it is as if it were said: "What was the reply of the messengers?" It was then said: ﴿They said﴾.

When they intended to single them out in rejecting what they had said, he qualified it with his words ﴿to them their messengers﴾, who were submitting, at the beginning of their speech, and not doing what they did in evading the answer, with "inna" (indeed), meaning: ﴿We are only humans like you﴾. We have no superiority over you by virtue of what our essences require, but sameness in humanity does not prevent some humans from being singled out over others by virtues. The "mithl" (likeness) is that which fills the place of another, such that if one observer saw it and then another observer saw the other, no difference would be found. ﴿But God﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs, ﴿bestows favour upon whom He wills﴾, that is, He bestows it upon him ﴿of His servants﴾, out of mercy from Him toward him, by preferring him over his like with what He apportions to him of distinctions, as you yourselves recognise. So they did not state explicitly what distinguished them, namely the attribute of prophethood, nor did they assign to themselves the bounty of God alone, but included themselves within the generality of "whom God wills." All of this was out of humility on their part and acknowledgment of servanthood. The "mann" (bounty) is a benefit by which one is cut off from misery; its root meaning is "cutting," and from it comes the phrase ﴿ghayr mamnun﴾ (never-ending/unceasing), and the "minna" (favour) cuts one off from the world.

(p-395) When they had explained the aspect of the difference, they followed it with an explanation of the excuse regarding what they were asked for, so they said: ﴿And it is not for us﴾, that is, it is not for us to show favour to you in anything that has not been permitted to us, with "wa mā" (and not) and "kāna" (it was) meaning: it is valid and proper ﴿for us to bring you any authority﴾ of what you propose in obstinacy, and that is the proof by which one dominates to nullify the doctrine of one who opposes the truth, other than the miracle by which prophethood is established, ﴿except by God's leave﴾, that is, by the release and deferment of the Supreme King. So we rely upon God regarding your affair: if He permits us to bring an authority, or does not permit it, whether you agree or disagree. ﴿And upon God﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs, and there is no command for anyone alongside Him alone, ﴿let the believers therefore put their trust﴾, that is, as a binding command. How much more so, then, the prophets.

Then they explained the reason for the obligation of *tawakkul* (reliance on God) in their words: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not rely upon Allah﴾, meaning, and what reason do we have, ﴿that we should not rely upon Allah﴾, the Lord of Majesty and Honor, ﴿while He has already guided us to our ways﴾, that is, He has made clear to us everything we should do and everything we should avoid. So there is no escape for us from any of that. We must therefore carry out all of His commands and refrain from all of His prohibitions. ﴿And we will surely bear patiently﴾, they emphasized it to deny that the Messenger, despite being alone, would endure their harm, given their large number and strength, ﴿whatever harm you cause us﴾. He used the past tense to indicate that they had pardoned their harm in the past and so did not repay them for it. This is an invitation (*istijlab*, drawing them in) to the repentance of those who harmed them. They turned away from the present tense because they were awaiting God's command regarding the future, since He might command them to fight or might command them to be patient. Then He said: ﴿You have harmed us﴾, that is, in that which we were commanded to do, whatever it might involve, because we rely upon Allah and do not accuse Him in His decree. ﴿And upon Allah﴾, that is, the One who alone possesses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿let those who rely [upon Him] rely﴾, those who know from themselves their own incapacity, whether they are believers or not. So they entrust some of their affairs to others so that those others may suffice them in it, but He is the One of all-encompassing knowledge and complete power, and everyone other than Him is powerless. Patience is the key to relief, and the one who brings about goodness is the one who absolutely delivers from distress. [And the truth] must inevitably become dominant and victorious, and falsehood must inevitably become defeated and subdued, even if the trial lasts long.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 13:

When this dialogue had concluded, and every fair-minded person had come to know from it what the Messengers possessed of forbearance (ḥilm), knowledge (ʿilm) and wisdom (ḥikmah), and what their opponents possessed of misguidance (ḍalāl), ignorance (jahl) and obstinacy (ʿinād), and since the discourse contained something that may have indicated its conclusion, the Exalted began another dialogue concerning them (p-397), linking it by conjunction to what had preceded, and said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to their messengers﴾, belittling those whom they regarded as having been reduced to seeking refuge in them, and emphasizing with an oath, owing to their sense that the one who sees the Lord's defense of His allies would deny it, by saying: "By Him by whom we swear! One of two things will certainly happen: ﴿We will surely expel you from our land﴾, i.e., the land over which we now have dominion, ﴿or you will return to our religion﴾, by ceasing your opposition to us as you were before claiming the mission." Thus the application of the word "religion" (millah) to their silence regarding them is, by their assumption, an instance of the naming of the whole by a part, as in the example ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ [Nuh: 7], and it is a metonymy (majāz mursal). So the messengers were patient with this, as they had been informed, relying upon their Lord, and they persisted in advising them by calling them to God. ﴿Then He revealed to them﴾, i.e., He spoke to them in secret, because of the threats of their peoples against them, singling them out with this, ﴿their Lord﴾, the Benefactor to them, the One upon whom they relied, to calm their hearts and console their souls. And He emphasized, for the one who looks at the multitude and strength of the disbelievers, against hesitation regarding the content of the report, especially if he is a disbeliever, saying: ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾, by virtue of the greatness that We possess, which necessitates the execution of the command. Destruction (ihlāk) is the removal of a thing to a place where perception cannot reach it. ﴿The wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those thoroughly steeped in wrongdoing. And perhaps we have been (p-398) reporting about some of those whom we described as disbelief, while it is one who was not thoroughly steeped in his disbelief, which is the greatest of wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 14:

﴿And We will surely settle you in the land after them﴾ — i.e., apart from them — ﴿the land﴾ — i.e., the land in its general sense, and specifically their land. He indicated the absence of permanence through the preposition, saying: ﴿after them﴾, meaning that We will make you inherit it, whether We have decreed their expulsion of you or not. It is as if it were said: Is this specific to them? It is said: No, [rather] ﴿that﴾ — i.e., the matter of lofty aim — ﴿is for whoever fears My standing﴾ — i.e., the place where one stands before Me when I call him to account, and what his outcome will be there. This is more emphatic than saying "whoever fears Me."

﴿And fears My threat﴾ — that his wrongdoer will surely be destroyed and He will settle the believer in his land after him. So rejoice in this promise from Allah, the Exalted.

"And they sought victory" over their enemies, so they prevailed and succeeded. "And every stubborn tyrant was disappointed" — so We destroyed them all. And for Us was the self-sufficiency and the praise after their destruction, as it was before it. 

Stubbornness (al-'inad): refusing the truth while knowing it, out of arrogance and insolence; one who "'anada" (deviated) from the truth, deviating (unud). Tyranny (al-jabriyyah): seeking elevation of rank with that which has no further limit in attribute; therefore it is a blame upon the servant insofar as he seeks what is not his.

Then He follows it with something that serves as evidence of his failure: that his course toward what lies ahead of him, namely the punishment, means he will inevitably fall into it while he is unaware. He expressed his heedlessness of it by His saying: ﴿Hell lies behind him﴾, meaning: he will certainly come to dwell in it.

Since the point is the mere existence of being given to drink of pus in general, He used the passive form in His saying ﴿and he will be given to drink﴾, meaning: in it, ﴿of water of pus (ṣadīd)﴾, which is the washings of the people of the Fire, like their festering matter and their blood.

﴿Yatajarra'uhu﴾ means he forces himself to swallow it little by little, because of its bitterness and heat, so he chokes on it and suffers from its severity what no one knows the measure of except Allah. ﴿Wa-la yakadu yusighuhu﴾ means he is not close to swallowing it, for ishagha (swallowing with ease) is drawing a thing down the throat with the soul accepting it. ﴿Wa-ya'tihi al-mawtu﴾ means the causes of death, such that if any one of them came to him in the world he would die. ﴿Min kulli makan﴾: al-makan (place) is a substance prepared for settling, so this is a metaphor meaning that there comes to him from hardships what would cause death to one who had been decreed to die. ﴿Wa-ma huwa bi-mayyit﴾ means he is not one for whom death is established at all.

Because We have decreed his life to continue, adding to his punishment; and death is an accident that is opposed to perception in the animal body. ﴿Wa-min wara'ihi﴾ means after this person, in the Day of Recompense, which is unavoidable, and We did not create the heavens and the earth except for it. ﴿Adhabun ghalizun﴾ means he will receive in that day, along with what We have already prepared for him in the world, while he is heedless of it (p-400), a punishment that comes from behind, so it will be more severe, as is the case with what comes suddenly; or the meaning is that after this punishment there is in Hell another punishment, whose harshness your minds cannot bear to be described as more than severe.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 18:

When he had finished with their disputations, and with what followed them, in which he made clear that nothing could spare them from His assault, he struck for them in that matter a parable, saying: ﴿The parable of those who disbelieve in their Lord is⦆ — here the word "parable" (mathal) is used figuratively for an attribute that is strange — ﴿...who disbelieve in their Lord,⦆ treating Him lightly. He likened one who sets out toward a matter but does not look to his own conduct in going toward it, and instead is deceived by one who led him astray from the path, so that he is taken far, far off, until he reaches ravines in which settling is impossible and from which return cannot be achieved, and so he perishes in ruin.

Since the distinction between a human being and nothingness lies only in deeds, he mentioned what is known from it: that the parable concerns their deeds, by way of answering one who seems to have asked: "What is their likeness?" So he said: ﴿Their deeds⦆ — that is, the noble acts they used to perform in the world, such as maintaining ties of kinship, emancipating slaves, ransoming captives, generosity and the like — ﴿on a day of reckoning.⦆ It is permissible for this to be a second subject (mubtada' thani), as al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said, and it together with its predicate is the predicate of the first subject, and it needs no connecting pronoun, because it is itself the parable, whose meaning is the attribute.

﴿Like ashes⦆ — that is, what fire has pulverized into dust-like powder — ﴿which the wind blows violently⦆ (p-401), that is, it hastens its movement with great force; and "wind" (rih) is a fine body fixed in the air, whose nature is to blow. The winds are five: the north wind (shimal), the south wind (janub), the east wind (saba), the west wind (dabur), and the mixed wind (nakba'). ﴿On a stormy day⦆ — that is, a day of intense wind — so that it scatters it in every direction, and they become such that ﴿they have no power⦆ — that is, on the Day of Recompense — ﴿over anything of what they earned.⦆ Since the matter here is one of testing deeds, He placed the phrase ﴿of what they earned⦆ first: what they earned in the world of their deeds, on that day, ﴿of anything⦆ — rather, it has gone off as scattered dust, because it was built on no foundation. Thus it is established, by what this entails, that those who disbelieved in their Lord and preferred the present life over the Hereafter are in far-reaching error. Indeed, ﴿that⦆ — that is, this matter of extreme monstrousness — ﴿is⦆ [that is, specifically] ﴿the far-reaching error⦆, from which its bearer cannot be able to recover.

When he mentioned the Hereafter at [the beginning of] the surah, he mentioned something that is established and not in dispute. Then he [drew] the discourse toward it here in this peculiar manner, and he followed it with the deeds of the disbelievers in the Hereafter. He then followed that with the proof for it, and for the fact that in wisdom nothing but nullification is fitting for the deeds of error. So he said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, ﴿created the heavens﴾, despite their greatness and height, ﴿and the earth﴾, despite the distance and vastness of its regions, ﴿in truth﴾, by a firm command, placing each thing of them in its place as wisdom requires, not by illusion and deception like magic. It is known that they are a container, and the contained, which is the thing intended in itself, can only be like its container or greater than it. So how could one suppose that He creates something in them in vain, such that if it is false He would not nullify it, or if it is true He would not establish it? Or how could one imagine that He, with the power to bring them both into existence from non-existence, and they being greater in creation and more exalted in status, is unable to restore those who are in them, who are weaker in affair and smaller in rank? Or [how could one imagine that] He created them by means of the truth, which is the restoration of people in a restoration by which they will be established and will remain in a permanence with no end after it? Thus it follows from this that He is of great power, and so He is such that ﴿if He wills, He can take you away﴾, that is, by some kind of taking away: death or other than it, ﴿and bring a new creation﴾ other than you, or bring you after you have perished, such that you return, as you are, a new creation. And the "jadid" (new) is that which has been cut off from work at the beginning. Its root is cutting; thus the "jidd" is the father of one's father, cut off from begetting by the father. And the "jadd" is the opposite of jest, by which one cuts the distance, sensorily or in meaning.

Translation of the passage:

﴿And that﴾ (the removal and bringing of a new creation), with ease, ﴿is not difficult for Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿to be impossible﴾, meaning that it is unattainable in any respect of impossibility, because it is not like the creation of the heavens and the earth, let alone being greater than that. So there is no basis for your saying ﴿Shall we show you a man who will inform you...﴾ [Saba: 7] and so on, because whoever has power over all possible things has no specialization in one thing over another. Thus it is established by this that their being far gone in error, which necessitates the ruin of their deeds, which are their means (of salvation), necessitates their destruction.

When this proof had established His power to restore them after death, He followed His words, *"They will have no power over anything of what they have earned"* (Ibrahim 14:18), with His words, as an explanation that the Resurrection is easy for Him and within His reach: *"And they will come forth"*, that is, on that Day. He expressed it in the past tense, which denotes what has occurred and been realized, because the reports of kings must be true, since they have power and are free from lying. How much more so for the King of kings! In this wording there is, for one who reflects deeply on the meaning, a stirring and awe of the soul that the present tense does not have. *"Before Allah"*, that is, the Supreme King, *"all together"*. They were in a state in which nothing of them was hidden from what is customary among them, because they had no cover. Indeed, *burz* (emerging) is the coming out of a thing from what it was mixed with to the point where the senses perceive it. *"And there will become apparent to them [from Allah]"* what they had not reckoned of the punishment, and their means will be cut off from them. *"Then the weak will say"*, that is, the followers (p-404) from among the people of misguidance, because they know that they are in His grip and have no refuge, rebuking their leaders [and reproaching them], confirming His words, may He be exalted: *"Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous"* (al-Zukhruf 43:67). *"To those who were arrogant"*, that is, who sought arrogance and claimed it, so they made others follow them in it until they became proud toward the messengers and their followers, though they had no right to that.

*"Indeed, we were"*, that is, a state that is like an innate disposition, *"for you followers"*, that is, those who followed you, or possessors of followers. So you were the cause of our misguidance. The custom of great leaders is to defend their followers who support them in their falsehoods. *"Then will you avail us in any measure"*, that is, will you repel *"from us a portion of the punishment of Allah"*, that is, He to whom all greatness belongs, so that His retribution cannot be endured. They used the expression "min" (some) with the first *min*, which is for diminution (partitive), after the partitive sense, and said: *"any portion"*, as if the punishment needed to take them, so they would be relieved by taking something other than them, to the point that it would pass them by if they repelled it from themselves. It is as though it were said: "Indeed, that is the custom of the leaders; so what did they say?" Then it was said: *"They will say"*, knowing that they have no ability to exercise any kind of control: *"We cannot avail you at all. Rather, each one is recompensed for what he did. Upon us is the sin of our misguidance in ourselves and our misguiding of you, and upon you is your misguidance and your defending us and strengthening our side, until we became arrogant"* (p-405) *"and so we were immersed in misguidance. Had Allah guided you until you followed the proofs that you heard, as we heard them, and had you left us, that would have broken something of our strength and weakened our might, and it would perhaps have been a cause of our guidance, just as, "Had Allah guided us"*, that is, the One who possesses all attributes of perfection, *"we would have guided you."* So it would have been for us the reward of our being guided and our guiding you, and for you the reward of your being guided and your strengthening us in that. But He did not guide us, so we went astray, and you were followers of us, so we misguided you.

Since what prompted their saying this was anguish, they said: *"It is all the same to us"*, that is, we and you, *"whether we rage"*, and *jaza'* is the unsettling of the soul upon the arrival of what distresses it, *"or whether we endure"*. Neither of them is of any benefit to us, because the matter is more grievous than that, for *"we have no place of escape"*. *Mahis* is suitable as a verbal noun, a time, and a place, meaning a place of escape and a removal from what is hated, on both interpretations. Nothing remains in the recompense but an increase of punishment through evil speech and the spreading of disgrace. This interrogative is not on its usual basis; rather, what is meant by it is to alert them that their situation is one about which questions should be asked and the matter should be repeated, so that they may refrain from the like of it.

[p. 406] Since Satan was the greatest of the arrogant, he was singled out for the answer in the singular, and it is said: ﴿And Satan said﴾, the first of those who were followed in error, ﴿Satan﴾, who is the head of the misleaders and the arrogant, the one decreed to distance and burning, ﴿when the matter had been decided﴾, by the fixing of one group for Paradise and another group for the Fire. This is an answer to the followers' words, submissive where submission no longer benefits and believing where the benefit of belief has passed. ﴿Indeed, God﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿promised you a promise of truth﴾, by sending to you messengers and sending down with them proofs and scriptures, in which He informed you that He is your Lord, the One, the Subduer, and He called you to Him after the devils had made you cling to falsehood. He gave glad tidings to those who responded and warned those who refused, with what He is able to do in the fullest sense of ability. So everything He said, reality conformed to, as you see, so He was truthful to you and fulfilled for you. ﴿And I promised you﴾, I, by what I adorned for you of "the sins from the whisperings," a promise of falsehood. ﴿But I broke it to you﴾, for I said nothing except that it was deviation. So you followed me, although I am your enemy, and you abandoned your Lord, while He is your Lord [and your Protector]. The verse is of the type of *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its counterpart omitted, and vice versa): He mentioned ﴿the promise of truth﴾ first as evidence for the omission of its opposite in the second place, and "I broke it to you" second as evidence for the omission of "your truthfulness" in the first place.

[p. 407] When he had explained his deceit, he explained how easily they were deceived, as an increase in their reproach, and so he said: ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾ in that matter, so there is no blame on me for that, because I did not have ﴿any authority over you﴾. He used the stronger form of negation and said: ﴿of authority﴾, that is, any domination, great or small, over anything at all. ﴿Except that﴾, that is, by ﴿calling you﴾ with the whispering which was a cause for strengthening your motives toward evil, ﴿and you responded﴾, that is, you brought about a response in the manner of one who seeks it and desires it, ﴿to me﴾, judging by your desires, turning away from the paths of the intellects and from the call of the advisers. Had you judged by your intellects, you would have followed the guides, because of the light in their path calling to it, and the darkness in the paths of others that blocks it, and the destructions that deter from it in this world and the next. He framed this in the form of an exception, although his calling was not from authority in any way, because authority is more specific than proof. Its meaning is a proof by which one dominates to nullify the doctrine of the opponent, indicating that they followed him while he had no power except this calling, which has no authority in it. They abandoned the call of the one who sent down to them, from every manifest authority, despite his threatening them with what He is able to do and striking them with some of it, and one who does such a thing is not to be blamed for anything other than himself. ﴿So do not﴾ [that is] ... since this has been established, it follows from it that I say to you: [do not] ﴿blame me, but blame yourselves﴾, because you are held accountable for your own earning, since you had power and choice, and you chose evil over good. It is known from this, with certainty, that each of us is preoccupied with the other by what he is recompensed with. So it is known that I ﴿am not your helper﴾, that is, I am not one who gives relief to you in what concerns you of the punishment, so that I would bring you what removes your cries from it, ﴿nor are you my helpers﴾ in what concerns me of it, because the means are cut off, by what has befallen of the punishment. Then he gave the reason for that with his words: ﴿Indeed, I disbelieved﴾, scorning, ﴿in your associating me﴾, that is, in your taking me as a partner with God.

Since their association did not extend over the whole of time, he used the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿before﴾, because that is a great wrong. Then he gave the reason for this cause with his words: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers﴾, that is, both groups in this attribute, ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, written for you of them, its measure determined, none of them avails the other anything, but each is confined to what has been decreed for him. The recounting of this exchange is to alert the listeners to consider the outcomes and to prepare for that day, before there is nothing but regret, the striking of hands together, and the biting of the hand.

When He mentioned the wrongdoers, He followed it with the mention of the believers. He said, using the passive voice because the entering is the primary intent: ﴿And those who believed will be admitted﴾. Al-idkhal (causing to enter) is, in its origin, transferring someone into an enclosure (p-٤٠٩). ﴿Those who believed﴾, meaning those who brought faith into being, and ﴿did righteous deeds﴾, as confirmation of their claim of faith, ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. He clarified that the water does not reach all of their land by using the preposition, so He said: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus they are always well-watered, their leaves and fruit never fall, so whoever enters them does not seek any substitute for them. ﴿Therein they will abide forever﴾.

Since dwelling is not pleasant except with the permission of the owner, He said: ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, who permitted them, through His nurturing and beneficence, to come out of darkness into light. It has been read as wa-udkhulu (﻿وأدخُلُ﻿), in the first person (of speech), and in that case there is a shift from saying "bi-idhni" (by My permission) to ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, to inform of the attribute that necessitates mercy, just as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1] ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾ [al-Kawthar: 2], and He did not say "to Us," it being the same. Of its similar form is ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1] ﴿that Allah may forgive you﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. Therefore one should not hastily deny anything that admits of a sound interpretation; rather, careful reflection is required. The matter is as the Imam Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni said in his book al-Muhtasib, in interpreting ﴿what descends from fear of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74] (p-٤١٠): the speech of the Arabs, for one who knows it [and who is that who knows it?], is subtler than magic, purer than the clear sight of the refined mind, more interlocking, each part falling upon another, and closer in supporting the supplementary to the obligatory.

﴿Their greeting﴾, i.e., among themselves, and the greeting of the angels to them. Tahiyyah (greeting) is receiving someone with honor in address, and so it is a manifestation of the nobility of the one addressed. ﴿Therein is peace﴾, i.e., well-being, safety, and permanence. The saying of one of them to another, "May Allah perpetuate your safety," and the like, is an announcement of the continuance of well-being, just as the state of the people of falsehood in the Fire is ruin and pains.

Now that it has been established from what preceded that the truth is what Allah has said, done, or permitted, and that falsehood is what occurs without His command, such as what is attributed to Satan or others in speech or action, and that it is not fitting in wisdom for Him to negate the truth or to leave falsehood in place, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾ [Yunus: 81], ﴿And Allah establishes the truth by His words﴾ [Yunus: 82], ﴿that He may establish the truth and nullify falsehood﴾ [al-Anfal: 8], and He, glory be to Him, related the speech of His friends, which is part of His speech, and so it is the most firmly established, the best, and the most fruitful of things, (p-٤١١) and the speech of His enemies, which is part of the speech of Satan, and so it is the most baseless and the most wicked of things, He, glory be to Him, brought that closer by means of an example (mathal, a comparison or proverb) familiar to its addressees, and said: ﴿Have you not considered﴾, i.e., O you who do not understand this example in its true understanding except through Him! ﴿how Allah has presented﴾, i.e., the One encompassing everything in power and knowledge, ﴿an example﴾, i.e., His course, such that its benefit is general. A mathal is a widely circulated saying in which the state of the second is likened to the state of the first. Then He explained it by His words: ﴿a good word﴾, i.e., one that gathers every kind of nobility, so there is nothing of wickedness in it, and that word is ﴿like a good tree﴾.

Since it cannot flourish except through stability, He said: ﴿Its root is firm﴾, i.e., well-established in the earth, safe from being uprooted by winds and the like, ﴿and its branches﴾ are high, rising, and swaying ”in“ the direction of ﴿the heaven﴾, owing to the goodness of its place of growth and the purity of its substance. So the verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting items are mentioned, each one implying the other): the mention of "firm" first indicates "high and rising" second, and the mention of "heaven" second indicates "earth" first.

When he had mentioned its state, he mentioned its fruit, saying: ﴿It gives its fruit﴾, i.e., its produce, by the goodness of its soil and the constancy of its irrigation, ﴿every time﴾, in the best manner of giving, because its height protected it from the putrefactions of [the earth] and the filth of dwellings, so its fruit was pure, free from the impurities of defilements.

Since a thing is not perfected except by the perfection of the one who nurtures it, He said: ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾. So it is such that no rational person would permit himself to cause its corruption, and whoever strives toward that is prevented by people of intellect, even if they must go as far as sacrificing their lives. Al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir and elsewhere, from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Tell me of a tree that is like the Muslim man, whose leaves do not fall, and [...] and [...], it gives its fruit every time.' Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: 'It came into my mind that it was the palm tree, but I saw Abu Bakr and 'Umar not speaking, so I disliked to speak. When they said nothing, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: It is the palm tree.' When we rose, I said to 'Umar: 'O father! By Allah, it had come into my mind that it was the palm tree.' He said: 'What prevented you from speaking?' He said: 'I did not see you speaking, so I disliked to speak.' 'Umar said: 'For you to have said it would have been dearer to me than such-and-such.'"

Then He, glorified is He, drew attention to the greatness of this parable so that one would turn to reflecting upon it, that its meaning might be known (and thus) it be adhered to. So He said: ﴿And Allah sets forth parables﴾, i.e., He who has complete encompassing knowledge, ﴿for the people﴾, i.e., those who need that because of the confusion of their opinions, for in striking them there is increased understanding and depiction of meanings. For pure meanings, when a suitable thing from the perceptible is mentioned, are imprinted upon the senses, the imagination and the estimative faculty, and are conceived; then these faculties abandon disputing about them, so complete understanding and arrival at the desired goal are attained, ﴿that they may remember﴾, i.e., so that their state becomes that of one for whom the utmost remembrance is hoped — by what the expression indicated. Thus this is like the words of the friends of Allah: their good word is the word of tawhid, than which nothing is more good, and it is the root of every firm happiness in their hearts, rooted in every vein of them. What caused its rooting was that its branches, which are the religious acts of the heart and the limbs, spread out, so that whenever [it is shaken], the one who shakes it gathers its fruits, which have no end, knowing that they are from the bounty of his Master, in which he has no making whatsoever, rather to Him, glorified is He, belongs the favour upon him in all of that. Just as a tree is not complete except with a firm root, an upright trunk and high branches, so too faith is not complete except with knowledge in the heart, speech of the tongue and action of the limbs.

Then He followed this with the likeness of the enemies, saying: ﴿And the likeness of an evil word﴾ [i.e., one deeply rooted in evil, with no good in it] ﴿is like an evil tree﴾

Since the destruction of harmful things and rest from their existence, in whatever state they are, is among the most beneficial matters, He used the passive form in His saying ﴿uprooted﴾, i.e., it was eradicated by pulling out its whole trunk from its root, ﴿from upon the earth﴾, according to the opinion of everyone who holds an opinion. Then He gave the reason for this in His saying ﴿it has no stability﴾, and He emphasized the negation with His saying ﴿no stability﴾, i.e., in the view of anyone who has even minimal intellect, because it has no benefit; rather, its existence is harmful even by occupying the earth. Likewise, the evil, false word has no permanence [at all], even if it rises for a time, because its argument is refuted, so its armies are defeated.

فَلَمّا بَرَزَ الكَلامُ إلى هَذَيْنَ المِثالَيْنِ، حَصَلَ التَّعَجُّبُ مِمَّنْ يَتْرُكُ مَمْثُولَ الأوَّلِ ويَفْعَلُ مَمْثُولَ الثّانِي، فَوَقَعَ التَّنْبِيهُ عَلى أنَّ ذَلِكَ بِفِعْلِ القاهِرِ، فَقالَ تَعالى - جَوابًا لِمَن كَأنَّهُ [قالَ]: إنَّ هَذا الصَّرِيحَ الحَقُّ، ثُمَّ إنّا نَجِدَ النُّفُوسَ مائِلَةً إلى الضَّلالِ، وطائِشَةً في أرْجاءِ المَحالِّ، فَكَيْفَ لَنا بِالِامْتِثالِ؟ ﴿Allah makes firm﴾ (p. 415) — that is, the One to whom belongs majesty and beauty — ﴿those who believe﴾, that is, those who brought this truth into being, even at its lowest degree, ﴿with the firm word﴾, that is, [which is] following the proof, ﴿in the life of this world﴾ by means like the previous attempts of His prophets, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, and He guides them at every question to the best of words, at the point where intellects go astray and thoughts are bewildered by the severity of the terrors. ﴿And Allah leads astray﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who are deeply immersed in wrongdoing, and He unsettles them because of their turning in the darknesses, which are such that their possessor is destined to misguidance and confusion, so they do what no sensible person would approve. The verse is of the type called *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned and each is left implicit in the other): it mentions firmness first as an indication of its opposite, and misguidance second as an indication of guidance first. ﴿And Allah does﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs, so He is not questioned about what He does, ﴿what He wills﴾, because all things are under His judgment and decree, and He is the Irresistible, the Subduer; so one should not be astonished at anything. In this is guidance toward turning to Him and casting the reins of need upon Him.

Al-Bukhari related in the Book of Tafsir and elsewhere, and Muslim at the end of the chapter on the description of Paradise and Hellfire, from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Muslim is questioned in the grave, he testifies that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah makes firm...﴾ the verse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 28:

When He, glorified be He, had informed that He alone is the One who acts, He followed it with the proof of that: the misguiding of those who exchanged the good word of tawhid (monotheism) for shirk (associating partners with God), and their being shaken, and the uprooting of their word. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾, and He indicated their distance from his station, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, by His saying: ﴿those who exchanged﴾. Tabdil (exchange) is making one thing take the place of another. ﴿The favour of God﴾, that is, the One who combines the attributes of perfection, which He bestowed upon them from the word of tawhid, and what He inherited for them from the religion of their father Isma'il, peace be upon him, and from all the worldly blessings, such as security of the land, facilitation of provision, and other than that, so that instead of thanking for them they made ﴿disbelief﴾, while they claim that they are the most thankful of people for kindness, the highest in aspiration in fulfilling obligations, and the furthest from ingratitude. ﴿And they caused their people﴾ by that ﴿to alight in the abode of destruction﴾, that is, ruin, while claiming that they are the most zealous of people in defending the neighbour, let alone the family. Al-Bukhari narrated in his Tafsir that they were the disbelievers of the people of Makkah. Al-Bawar (destruction) is excessive ruin, and al-Ihlal (causing to alight) is making a thing be in a place. If it is a substance, then it is ihlal mujawara (alighting beside), and if it is an accident, then it is ihlal mudakhala (alighting within).

Since he had indicated that it is a place of destruction, he clarified it in a way that conveys that it confronts them with scowling faces, just as they used to meet the friends of Allah among the messengers and others with that same attitude. So he said: ﴿Jahannam﴾ (Hell), while ﴿they will burn in it﴾, that is, they will directly experience its heat along with their being immersed in it, with its flames turning upon them. Since the implied meaning was: "Then evil is the abode they made for themselves and their people," he followed it with His saying: ﴿And evil is the settlement﴾ (p-417), that place to which they had brought them down.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 30:

When this act was that of one who has no intellect, he clarified it by His saying: ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾, whom they know to have no partner in their creation or in their provision, because He alone possesses all perfection, ﴿so that they may lead [others] astray﴾. He said: "so that they may lead [others] astray," meaning by themselves, according to the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, and that they may lead others astray, according to the reading of the rest [of the Readers], ﴿from His way﴾. For they, if they were intelligent, [then] they know that this is a necessary consequence of their act, so they intend it.
