Otherwise they have no intellects, for no one proceeds to something whose outcome is unknown except a fool. Yet they claim that they are the most perceptive of people, the purest of intellects, the most penetrating in thought, and the firmest in opinions. So who among them guides [others] to the path of salvation, and who warns them against the paths of destruction? This is in addition to the incurable disease into which they have cast themselves.

Since it has been established that they are opposed to everything they claim, and so they are deserving of turning away from them, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) would be inclined to say: "What should I do with them, when You have commanded me to bring them out to Your path?" He was commanded to crush their necks by informing them that what has led them astray of blessings is only a gradual lure (istidraj). So He said: "Say" (qul), meaning as a threat to them, for they do not doubt your words even though they are obstinate: ﴿Enjoy yourselves﴾, and go to extremes in the acts of cattle as much as you are able, for that will harm you and not benefit you, ﴿for indeed your destination is﴾, that is, your ultimate return, ﴿to the Fire﴾, because of your enjoyment in this manner.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 31:

When He had mentioned their disbelief and their straying from the Way, and that He had commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them, and this was something that stirs the soul of the listener to attend to what is said to those who have renounced rivals, and since the firmest handholds of the Way after faith, and the most comprehensive of them, are the prayer (ṣalāh), which forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and spending (infāq), which encompasses all forms of righteousness, He commanded him to urge His allies to turn toward what His enemies have turned away from, and to turn away from what they have turned toward in taking pleasure in it. So He said: ﴿Say to My servants﴾. He described them with the most noble of their attributes, and attributed them to His noble pronoun, to make them beloved to Him, and then He followed this description with what corresponds to it of their submission to their Lord, saying: ﴿who have believed﴾, meaning, who have brought this attribute into being.

Since His saying, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is the best of speech, it polishes the rust of hearts and necessitates the refinement of souls, He said, in a decisive manner: ﴿that they establish the prayer﴾, which is the purification of strength and the connection of the servant to his Lord, ﴿and spend﴾. He lightened the burden on them by His saying: ﴿out of what We have provided them﴾, meaning, by Our greatness, so it is Ours, not theirs, from the kinds of expenditure that uphold His laws, such as charities and others, in perfecting what is between them and Him [of the means], so that they may rescue their own souls from the Fire. He limited Himself to these two traits because nothing else had been made obligatory in Makkah apart from them, together with their great merit and comprehensiveness. Perhaps it was phrased in the form of a conditional as a reminder to them that the mere saying of His, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is the strongest of means, so it is incumbent upon them not to lag behind it at all. Then He indicated constancy in these two qualities by His saying: ﴿secretly and openly﴾. It is possible that by "secretly" is meant the voluntary acts, and by "openly" the obligatory ones. Then He warned those who neglect His service of the Day on which turning away from Him was the cause of straying, saying, pointing with the preposition to the brevity of the period of their deeds: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾, meaning, a Day of immense greatness, unlike any of the days you know, ﴿in which there is no trade﴾ by which a captive might ransom himself, ﴿nor friendship﴾, meaning, companionships and affections from which intercession or help would arise. It is the plural of khullah, like qillah and qilal, or it is a verbal noun. This indicates that neither of them will be a cause of deliverance for one who is ruined.

When He negated all the means of benefit in the world on that Day, it was as if it were asked: "What is the judgment concerning it, that it proceeds in a course we do not know?" So it was said: "Allah," that is, the Supreme King, who encompasses everything. Then He followed this with attributes that point to what the Messengers called to concerning His oneness (*wahdaniyyah*), what they were informed of concerning His power over everything, so that no one can overpower Him, and concerning the return (*ma'ad*), and concerning His self-sufficiency, so that He does not engage in exchange. He said: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and they are greater in creation than you and greater in status. Then He followed this with the matter most indicative of the restoration, together with the great favor that by it there is life, so He said: ﴿and sent down water from the sky﴾.

Since that was the cause of growth, He said: ﴿and brought forth thereby﴾, that is, by the water from which He made every living thing, ﴿fruits as provision for you﴾, that is, of trees and other things, after the dryness of the earth and the withering of its plants. This is not less than the bringing to life of the dead. Then He followed it with what He stored in the earth of the waters of the seas and rivers, [and mentioned the most general of what appears from the seas], so He said: ﴿And He subjected for you the ships﴾, and He gave the reason for that in His saying: ﴿to run upon the sea﴾. Since that was a matter striking to the intellect, He clarified its greatness by His saying: ﴿by His command﴾. Since the rivers are among the great blessings after the blessing of the seas, He said: ﴿And He subjected for you the rivers﴾.

Then He followed it with what made it a cause for the perfect disposition and ripening of the fruits watered by the water [descending] from the sky and springing from the earth. So He said: ﴿And He subjected to you the sun and the moon﴾, [while] being ﴿constant﴾, meaning in their course and their giving of light, and in what arises from them of improvement by cooking and ripening in minerals, plants and animals. Al-Rummani said: al-da'ub (constancy) is the passing of a thing in its work in a continuous habitual manner. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned what arises from the presence and absence of the sun, so He said: ﴿And He subjected to you the night﴾, meaning the one whose sign is the moon, ﴿and the day﴾ [meaning] the one whose sign is the sun, each of them coming into existence after the passing of the other. Had either of them been perpetual, the state would have been disrupted by the absence of plants and animals, as is the case in places where the sun does not set in the south and where it does not rise in the north.

Then he generalized after having specified, saying: ﴿and He gave you﴾.

Since perfection can only be found in Paradise, He said: ﴿of all that you asked Him for﴾, meaning whatever you have need of, for you are asking for it in potential. Then he confirmed the aspect of greatness by positing what makes one incapable, saying: ﴿And if you count﴾, O people, all of you, ﴿the favour of Allah﴾, meaning you attempt to count the bounties of the Sovereign Most High, to whom belongs absolute perfection, or you undertake to enumerate them. He expressed it as "favour" as a guidance toward inferring the Originator from the effect. ﴿You will not be able to number them﴾, meaning you will not be able to encompass them, nor know how to count them with pebbles (al-hasa) corresponding to them, if you were to count them with them, as was the custom of the Arabs, or you would not find among pebbles enough to fulfil their number. This is in regard to a single favour, so how about what exceeds it! This is the explanation of His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 2]. It has become clear through it that nothing exists except that it is the possession of Allah, let alone that there exists anything that owes Him a debt, let alone something similar to Him. Thus it is established that there is no sale nor friendship on the Day of the Reckoning of the servants. And the approach to incapacity to count, for the sake of understanding, is that safety from every disease which the physicians have mentioned in their books — despite their multiplicity and length — is a favour upon the servant, and that is difficult to confine. And all that they have mentioned explicitly, relative to what falls under their universal principles implicitly, is little. How then about what Allah has not made them aware of, nor guided them in any way to it? This is regarding the body. As for the intellect, safety from every deviant belief and every false religion that inclines toward error is likewise; and none can enumerate that except the Creator of thought and the Originator of natural disposition, glorified is He; how mighty He is and how great is His station!

And since most of this surah is concerned with explaining the disbelievers and their state, and explaining that most of creation is perishing and turning away from what comes to them of the favour of guidance through the hands of the Messengers, the callers to Him who possesses all the blessings for the good life with the happiness of both abodes, He concluded the verse by explaining the attributes of humankind that necessitated that, saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind﴾, meaning this species, because of its attachment to itself, its forgetfulness of what benefits and harms it, and its agitation due to what distresses and gladdens it, ﴿is surely a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾, meaning exceedingly wrong-doing and ungrateful, in that it neglects thankfulness and goes beyond it to disbelief. He concluded a similar matter in [Surat an-Nahl] with ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nahl: 18], because that is the surah of blessings, which began with the prohibition of hastening the punishment, since mercy precedes; and from mercy is granting people respite and letting them enjoy benefits. So the estimate there is: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you will not be able to number them; indeed, mankind is surely a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾, but their Lord does not hasten to punish them, for He is Forgiving and Merciful. As for this surah, it began with the statement that people are in darknesses.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 35:

When the command concerning what was to be said to the one who is ungrateful for the blessing and to the one who is thankful for it, along with its cause and its proof, had been completed, and it became clear that He is the Creator of all existing things and their Lord, so that it is not at all valid that any of them be a partner, He, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, was commanded to remind them of the Days of Allah (ayyam Allah) concerning their father Ibrahim (peace be upon him), to show that they had exchanged the blessing for wrongdoing and disbelief on their part, in a style that points to the resurrection, indicating the obligation of their disavowal of the idols, since their whole state in them was blind imitation of the fathers, and he (Ibrahim) was the greatest of their fathers, and indicating what he (Ibrahim) prescribed for them of establishing the prayer and thanking Him for His blessings through spending and otherwise. So He said, rebuking them, while contrary to clear reason and decisive transmission, [and] disobeying their greatest father, coupling it with ﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾ [Ibrahim: 31] or with ﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾ [Ibrahim: 6]: ﴿And when﴾, that is, recount to them, as a reminder of the Days of Allah, the account of Ibrahim when ﴿Ibrahim said, "My Lord"﴾, that is, O You who have done me good by answering my supplication, in making the barren valley where I placed my son into a great city.

Since the context concerns the expulsion of the messengers from their places, and that implies that the place from which expulsion occurs is a town in which one dwells, and He, glorified is He, followed this by saying that those who opposed them had exchanged Allah's blessing, by which He made it a safe place after making it a town, by what they produced in it of intimidation toward the best of its people, and of threats toward those on whom He had bestowed every good in it, it was most fitting to define it, so He said: ﴿Make this town﴾ [that is] the one from which they wish to expel the Messenger ﴿secure﴾, that is, possessing security through the safety of its people. It seems this supplication was uttered by him after people had settled in Makkah and it had become a city. What is in al-Baqarah was when he placed his son with his mother in a place empty of any inhabitant, so he prayed that Allah make it a town, and that He make it afterward described as secure, and security is the tranquility of the soul in the removal of harm.

When he prayed for security from corruption of wealth and bodies, he followed it with a prayer for security [from] corruption of religion, so he said: ﴿And keep me and my sons﴾, that is, turn me away, ﴿and my sons﴾, that is, my offspring, and he omitted the daughters, indicating independence, since they are always subordinate, ﴿from worshipping﴾, that is, a continuous worship that would make the Fire obligatory, ﴿idols﴾, that is, place us on a side other than the side of their worship. And the sanam is that which is carved in the form of a human; and whatever is carved in other than the form of a human is a wathan, as al-Tabari said, from Mujahid;

Then he showed the increased concern with the matter of the idols by repeating the call, and he dropped the particle, as an increase in supplication, by describing himself as among those who are near to Him and devoted to Him, glorified is He, giving the reason for what precedes it, in his saying: ﴿My Lord﴾, using the singular form of the one addressed, so that the speech would be (ال)[the single] in one arrangement (nizam). ﴿Indeed they have led astray﴾ is a figurative attribution (isnad majazi, a figurative ascription of an action), whose relation (ʿalaqah) is causation, ﴿many of the people. Whoever﴾, meaning: as a consequence of my hatred for them, I say: whoever "follows me" among all people in avoiding them, ﴿then he is of me﴾, meaning of my party, because he is on my path and my religion. So grant me what You promised me of success. ﴿And whoever disobeys me﴾, going astray through them, then he has deserved the Fire. If You punish him, then they are Your servants, and if You forgive him, then You are entitled to that, because You may do whatever You will. ﴿Indeed You are Forgiving﴾, meaning of far-reaching concealment, ﴿Merciful﴾, meaning of far-reaching honour, after concealing sins; (p-٤٢٦) and he emphasised it to inform of the increase in his desire for pardon, because nothing of His might or His wisdom, glorified is He, is diminished by it, as the supplication of Jesus, peace be upon him, in al-Ma'idah indicated.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 37:

When he (Abraham) prayed for the removal of the corruptions arising from the two kinds, mankind and the devils, by making the city secure and by (granting) its faith, he mentioned the cause that moved him to single it out for this, seeking to attract benefits. So he said: "Our Lord," that is, O Lord, and Lord of those whom You have decreed will follow me, by Your nurturing us in the best nurture: ﴿I have settled﴾. It seems that Allah, glory be to Him, had informed him that his offspring would multiply until they would be like the stars, and this was after the glad tidings of Isaac, peace be upon him. So he said: ﴿of my offspring﴾. He emphasised it (with the particle "min" and the phrase) as an alert that, because it is in a manner that no one would permit, it is hardly to be believed. And to inform (them) that he desires it, (he said) "in a valley" which is Makkah the Honoured, because it lies in a low expanse between mountains through which floods flow, ﴿without cultivation﴾.

When he negated from it the worldly provision, he affirmed for it the otherworldly one, as an indication that the two abodes are rival co-wives that cannot be combined. It seems this supplication was after his building the House, as the allusion to it was also previously made by the definition of the city. So he said: ﴿at Your Sacred House﴾, that is, the one which You have made sacred to be approached and whom You have protected with awe, so that no one other than You possesses it. (p-427) And He made for it a sacred precinct in which the wild beasts and birds are safe. Settling (al-sukna) means taking a dwelling to which one resorts whenever one wishes. The valley (al-wadi) is the foot of a great mountain, and from it rivers are called awdiyah (valleys), because their banks are like mountains for them. And the crop (al-zar') is a plant that spreads without a stalk. Then he explained his purpose in settling them there, and so he said: "Our Lord," that is, O You who are good to us, ﴿that they may establish the prayer﴾. I settled them in this described valley only for this purpose, which is incompatible with the worship of other than You, and because the most worthy of people to establish it are those present at the House toward which it is directed.

Since their occupation with worship and their being in that valley were two matters remote from the means of livelihood, there followed from it his saying: ﴿so make hearts﴾, that is, hearts burning with longing ﴿of people﴾, that is, of the hearts of those who are fit for agitation, their burning with longing preventing their agitation, ﴿incline﴾, that is, they aim toward them and hasten to them with desire and longing, like the hastening of one who descends from a height. And he increased the meaning in clarity and emphasised it with the particle of extremity, which indicates distance, because the more distant the target of a thing, the more forceful its impact. So he said: ﴿towards them﴾. [And when he prayed for them regarding religion, he prayed for them regarding provision, which includes a supplication for their neighbours, so he said]: ﴿and provide for them﴾, that is, through the hand of those who incline towards them ﴿with fruits﴾, that is, those which You have caused to grow in their lands. And he stated the appropriate cause with his saying: ﴿so that they may be thankful﴾, that is, so that their condition would be the condition of those from whom thankfulness is hoped for, because of Your blessings, which break the customary order, that they see in that remote place, far from abundance, were it not for Your care [so that they would occupy themselves with Your worship, because of Your enriching] them and Your kindness towards them. And Allah answered his supplication. So the verse is a reminder to Quraysh of these great blessings upon them, by the blessing of their greatest forefather, who forbade the worship of idols.

"Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal and what we declare." Having finished with the supplication for what matters most, namely the preservation of the original nature (al-fitrah al-ula), which inclines the resolves toward dwelling in the abode of intimacy, and with the provision of sustenance for them, which produces gratitude through spending the surplus, and having made clear that they had opposed their greatest forefather in all the benefits he intended for them, He followed this with what urges sincerity (al-ikhlas) in that and in other matters, for Him and for others, so that it may be more successful in attaining the goal through the guarantee of felicity, especially with the repetition of the call, which indicates greater humble supplication. So He said: "Our Lord" (rabbana), meaning, O You who do good to us, the Owner of all our affairs, ﴿Indeed You know what﴾, meaning all that (p-429) ﴿we conceal and what we declare﴾. Then He pointed to the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, saying: ﴿And nothing is hidden from Allah﴾, meaning He who encompasses everything in power and knowledge. He emphasized the negation, saying: ﴿of anything﴾, of that or of anything else, ﴿on the earth﴾. Since this was in the context of emphasis, He repeated the negator for confirmation, saying: ﴿nor in the heaven﴾. That is, He has no need to be informed through supplication; supplication is only for the manifestation of servitude. The noun of genus (ism al-jins) encompasses what is above one. Among the benefits of expressing it in the singular is the indication that He who encompasses everything in the two opposites, without one of them veiling Him from the other, is likewise encompassing of what is other than them, without any difference.

(p-430) When the supplication he made, seeking that he be free from the defilement of polytheism, was complete, and it had become clear through his placing it first that the most important of matters is disavowal of it, he followed it with praise for the blessings Allah had provided, and what accompanies that of indication to the obligation of gratitude. So he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿who has granted me﴾. The grant (hibah) is a gift of ownership without a contract, a favour from Him to "me" while I was [elevated] ﴿in old age﴾, and having attained it despite despairing of children: "Ishmael", whom He has settled here, and "Isaac". This indicates what I earlier understood, that this supplication came after the building of the House and his being reassured by Isaac, peace be upon him. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that his age at the birth of Ishmael, peace be upon him, was ninety-nine years, and at the birth of Isaac, peace be upon him, was one hundred and twelve years.

Since the coming of a child [to him] at an age when one such as he does not beget was unusual, and all that he had asked [for] of extraordinary things, his child's existence was barely credible, he indicated this by emphasizing his words: ﴿Indeed my Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to me, ﴿is All-Hearer of supplication﴾, that is, it is in His nature to answer supplication in the most eloquent manner, an allusion to rivals and an indication of what his regret over barrenness implied. Earlier, in [Surat al-Baqarah], it was mentioned from the Torah that when his nephew [Lot] was freed from captivity, God said [to him]: "O Abraham! I will support you and help you, for your reward has become great." Abram said: "O Lord my God! What will You give me, since I am departing this world without offspring, and my heir will be Eliezer, my servant of Damascus?" The Lord said to him: "This one will not inherit you, but your son who comes from your loins, he will inherit you." And He said to him: "Look up to the sky and count the stars, if you are able to count them; so shall your descendants be." Abram then believed in Allah.

When the praise for the blessing was complete, following the prayer to be kept free of the things that undo happiness, and this was concluded with praise for the answering of the prayer, he seized the opportunity to follow it with a prayer to adorn himself with the adornment of worship. He had said that this was his aim when he settled some of his offspring [in the valley], and then that he would establish it. This points to how difficult it is for the self to perform it, except with God's help. So he said: ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, O You who brought me into being, the Owner of my affair, ﴿make me one who establishes the prayer (ṣalāh)﴾, that is, this form of worship, which indicates the utmost humility, and make me constant in maintaining it. It seems God the Exalted had informed him that some of his offspring would disbelieve, so out of courtesy (adab) he said: ﴿and from my offspring﴾.

Since prayer is the greatest of the pillars after faith, he made the pronoun singular for the supplication for it, drawing near to God the Exalted by the blessings He had bestowed on him, which He had not bestowed on anyone else in his time, as he indicated by the name "Lord." [Then he added] to his entreaty by saying: "Our Lord," that is, O You who are good to us. He made the pronoun he added to it plural, with regard to those among his offspring who would follow him, because what comes after it is another statement. That is: My Lord, and the Lord of those whom You have granted success, by Your nurturing and Your goodness, to establish the prayer from my offspring. ﴿And accept my supplication﴾, all of it, with this and other things, by making it accepted, making one who is as though he were eager for it and captivated by it.

Since man, however hard he strives, is the seat of inability, which necessarily brings shortcoming and so needs covering, He said, pointing to this: ﴿Our Lord﴾, that is, O Owner of our affairs, the One who manages us, ﴿forgive me﴾. Then He joined with him the nearest of people to him and the most deserving of his gratitude, saying: ﴿and my parents﴾. His seeking forgiveness for them was before he knew that his father had died an unbeliever. From the context it is known that when he was alone he used the singular pronoun, and when a dual form that can take the plural precedes him, the plural is used if what follows is independent. Then he included everyone who followed him in religion, of his offspring and others, saying: ﴿and for the believers﴾, that is, those firmly rooted in the description, ﴿on the day when the reckoning will take place﴾, that is, when it will become manifest and be realized in its most exalted aspects.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 42:

When He concluded His supplication with the Day of Reckoning, which requires remembering it for every happiness and forgetting it for every wretchedness, He mentioned some of what occurs on it, returning to what had passed concerning the conditions of the Day of Resurrection in the best manner. He said, conjoining it [to His saying] ﴿Say to My servants﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], and the aim is exalted: a threat to the people of wrongdoing through associating partners with Allah and other things. He addressed [the leader] who cannot be made to do this, so that it would fall more effectively upon the hearts of others: ﴿And do not think that Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King who is the most just of judges.

Since belief in the abandonment of reckoning entails attributing to the Judge incapacity, foolishness, or heedlessness, and since He had established His power and wisdom in this surah and elsewhere, exalting Himself above heedlessness, so that those who deny resurrection would awaken from their heedlessness, He said: "heedless." Heedlessness (al-ghaflah) is the departure of meaning from the self. ﴿of what the wrongdoers do﴾, those who have exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief, so they became deeply rooted in wrongdoing, even though the basis of their wrongdoing is intellectual doubts which they set up. It is as if it were said: "What then does He do to them?" He said: ﴿He only delays them﴾, that is, He delays their reckoning, down to the smallest detail, whether they are punished in this world or not, ﴿until a Day when the eyes will stare﴾, that is, they will be opened wide such that there will be no blinking of eyes in it [on the part of] them, ﴿in which﴾ [i.e. the Day], ﴿the eyes﴾, that is, while they are in the state of...

﴿مُهْطِعِينَ﴾ means hastening with the utmost speed toward the place to which they were called, [in fear] and anguish, while their eyes are fixed on the caller, not turning away from him to anything else. ﴿مُقْنِعِي رُءُوسِهِمْ﴾ means raising their heads and holding them erect, gazing in humiliation and submission toward one direction, the direction of the caller, not turning right or left (p-434). This is a metaphor for the utmost degree of abasement and debasement. Then he followed this with something that reinforces it, explicitly expressing the sense of fixed, staring gaze, saying: ﴿لا يَرْتَدُّ إلَيْهِمْ طَرْفُهُمْ﴾, "their glance does not return to them." Since their eyes, in their state of blinking and stillness, were nearly alike, he used the singular and said ﴿طَرْفُهُمْ﴾. Rather, their eyes are fixed, constantly open, not blinking, like the dying person, because of the terror that afflicts their owners. ﴿وأفْئِدَتُهُمْ﴾ is the plural of fu'ad (الفؤاد), the organ which by nature is heated by anger. In al-Qamus (the classical Arabic lexicon) it is said: al-tafa'ud (التَّفَؤُّد) means burning and blazing, and from it comes fu'ad, which is masculine when meaning the heart, and its plural is af'idah (أفْئِدَة).

﴿هَواءٌ﴾ means empty and void, having nothing in it of the boldness and pride which they display now. As Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

Is it not that you should convey to Abu Sufyan from me,
For you are hollow, a coward, and void.

Al-hawa' (الهواء) is the empty space not occupied by bodies, and al-nakhb (النخب) is the coward; likewise al-hawa' (in the sense of a coward), as stated in al-Qamus. So warn them of [the terrors of] that Day, for nothing of the arrogance and haughtiness in which they now persist will remain with them on it.

[p-435] ﴿And warn﴾, that is, O Muhammad, ﴿the people﴾ all of them, about what will befall them ﴿on the day the punishment comes to them﴾, when the veil is lifted from them by death or by resurrection.

Since, at the coming of the punishment before death, they are not wholly broken, he made clear that they are then otherwise. So he said, conjoining it to "yaʾtīhim" (comes to them): ﴿Then those who did wrong will say﴾, that is, those who brought about this attribute, even in its slightest degree, among themselves and among others, because the punishment came without respite. What they used to boast of, such as pride, zeal, haughtiness and arrogance, has left them, because of the terrors they see, which they cannot withstand and have no patience for: ﴿Our Lord﴾, O You who are good to us in creation, provision and nurture, ﴿delay us﴾, that is, grant us respite ﴿to a near term﴾. For if You delay us until then, ﴿we will answer Your call﴾, that is, by way of making amends for what we neglected. Answering means firmly resolving to agree with the one who calls, by will. ﴿And follow the messengers﴾ with the utmost eagerness. Then it will be said to them: when God's term comes, it is not delayed. Did you not used to say that the bonds of your patience do not loosen and the edge of your resolve does not dull? ﴿Had you not been﴾, that is, in a state in which you had full capacity, ﴿sworn﴾, that is, out of ignorance and folly, or out of wickedness and insolence.

Since the time of their oath did not encompass all of time, he said ﴿before﴾ [p-436]. He explained the answer they swore to by stating the meaning of their words, not their exact wording, so that the intended meaning would be explicit and free of ambiguity, which would not be the case had it been said, "What is for us?" He said: ﴿What is for you﴾, and he emphasized the negation by saying ﴿no cessation﴾ from what you are upon of disbelief and refusal to submit to faith, or from this world to the Hereafter, or from your dwellings in which you live. This is a metaphor for the firmness of the matter and for disregard of the opponent, whoever he may be.

And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, that is, by placing things in other than their proper places, as you have done, and it became clear to you (tabayyana lakum), that is, in the utmost clarity, through report and direct observation, [how] We dealt with them.

Since the state of one of them was utterly astonishing, He drew attention with the interrogative, indicating that he is worthy of being asked about, so He said: ﴿How We dealt with them﴾, that is, in accordance with Our greatness, when We took vengeance upon them, [yet] you did not take warning from their circumstances. ﴿And We set forth for you the parables﴾, that is, by what We have of greatness, ﴿clear parables﴾, showing that the custom of God has run, and you will not find any change in the custom of God (Qur'an 35:43), that just as the name of wrongdoing gathers the wrongdoers, the mark of destruction gathers them. So We combined for you the two paths of warning: hearing and sight. Then you did not benefit from either of them.

"And" the situation being that it has become clear to you that when We did to them what We did, ﴿they had plotted their plot﴾, meaning the severe, great plot in which they exhausted their effort, such that they had no other scheme left besides it, in order to strengthen disbelief and nullify the truth. Makr (plotting) is turning someone toward harm by way of stratagem.

"And" the situation being that it is "with Allah" — meaning, the One whose knowledge and power encompass all things — ﴿their plot﴾ is His alone, and He is knowing of it in all its aspects, however subtle it may be, and able to nullify it, however great it may be. ﴿And even if their plot was﴾ of such strength and magnitude "that the mountains would be moved" — "li-tazūla," meaning in order that the mountains would be moved ﴿by it﴾. The sense on the reading with a fatha on the first lām and a rafʿ on the second is: "even if their plot was such that the mountains would be moved by it." The two meanings are close. It was also said that "in" (in) is negative, and the lām is for emphasizing the negation, and "the mountains" are the signs (āyāt) and the sharīʿas (sharāʾiʿ), rather, they are more firmly established.

And since this has been established regarding His knowledge and power, the following is said as its consequence. As has been mentioned earlier, the intended addressee is the community, since the matter must reach every level of them. It is addressed to the head (the leader of the community) so that it would have a stronger effect on their hearts: ﴿So do not think that Allah (p. 438)—that is, the One to whom all perfection belongs—would fail His promise to His messengers﴾, for whoever thinks such a thing is deficient in intellect, [namely, thinking that He would fail] in that He would grant might to His allies, humiliate His enemies, destroy them for their wrongdoing, and settle His allies in the land after them. Then He gave the reason for this in His saying, emphasizing it because the great number of opponents and their power over the passing of days exposes the listener to denial: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the Possessor of majesty and generosity, is ﴿"Almighty"﴾, that is, He is able and cannot be overcome, ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾ against whoever opposes His command.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 48:

When the greatness of that Day, on which the eyes will stare fixedly, was established, and it was the greatest day on which retribution would manifest, He clarified it with His saying: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens [as well]﴾. That is, a strange and magnificent alteration, "the earth," i.e., this kind, ﴿other than the earth﴾ [i.e., the one] that you know, ﴿and the heavens﴾, after the scattering of their stars, their cleaving asunder, and other matters of their state. And tabdil (alteration) is the changing of a thing or its attribute into a substitute. ﴿And they will come forth﴾, i.e., the wrongdoers who used to say that they would not be presented before Allah for reckoning. And buruz (coming forth) is the appearance of a person from that which he had been concealed by, ﴿before Allah﴾, i.e., the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿the One, the Subduer﴾, the One who has no partner, the One whom nothing can repel from His will. Thus, by that coming forth, they will be in a state where they have no doubt that nothing hidden of them is concealed. As for the believers, they had always known this. (p-439) Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed...﴾ the verse. I said: O Messenger of Allah, then where will people be on that day? He said: 'On the Sirat.'"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 14, verse 49:

When he mentioned their emergence [before Him], he mentioned their condition in that emergence, saying: ﴿And you will see the criminals﴾ [i.e., and you see them], but [the verb] was expressed [as "you will see"] because of the multiplicity of their attributes which made disgrace necessary for them. And ijram (criminality, guilt) is the cutting off of what is permissible in action by doing what is not permissible. ﴿On that Day﴾, i.e., when these great matters [have come to pass], ﴿bound together﴾, i.e., each of them gathered together with his counterpart, or their hands gathered to their necks, a gathering in which there is severity and constriction, ﴿in shackles﴾, i.e., chains. What is meant here is the fetters (aghlal), i.e., the chains that gather the hands [in them] to the necks, and they are coupled in them together with their likes;

Then he explained the purpose of these acts on that day, saying, expressing it through "recompense" and "earning" (kasb), which is the locus of obligation and the expectation of benefit, because the context of subjugation (siyaq al-qahr) requires both: ﴿That Allah may recompense﴾, that is, the One to whom all perfection belongs, ﴿every soul﴾, whether obedient or disobedient. And since the matter is magnified by attributing the recompense to the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam), which gathers all the attributes of perfection, this requires that the earning itself be the recompense, because that is more wondrous and more precise in craftsmanship and more skilled at fashioning it with whatever fitting forms are beautiful when the reward is intended, and ugly when punishment is intended. For this reason he omitted the preposition bi- (which will be mentioned in "Ha Mim, the Believer") and said: ﴿what it earned﴾. Recompense (al-jaza') is the matching of an action with what it requires of good or evil; and earning (al-kasb) is doing what brings about a benefit or by which a harm is averted. And among the recompense of the believer is the punishment of whoever opposes him for the sake of Allah.

And since the reckoning of every soul is deserving of being regarded as great, he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses absolute encompassment, ﴿is swift in reckoning﴾, meaning that the reckoning of one soul does not preoccupy Him from the reckoning of another, nor one affair from another affair.

[p. 442] When this surah encompassed what has struck your ear of these admonitions, parables, and wisdoms, which left the eloquent speechless, silenced the articulate, and dazzled the intellects, He, glory be to Him, summarized it with what is fit to serve as a title for the whole Qur'an, saying: ﴿This﴾, that is, the Book by which people come out of darkness into light, ﴿is a message﴾, that is, sufficient to the utmost degree in conveying [the truth], ﴿for mankind﴾, so that through it they may reach Allah by adorning themselves with the virtues required to traverse His upright path. The root *balagha* (بَلَغَ), in whatever arrangement it occurs, revolves around arrival, and it sometimes implies strength and sometimes the exhaustion arising from weakness. *Balagha al-makan* balaghan means he reached that place; *balagha al-rajul* (كَعَنِيَ) means the man exerted himself to exhaustion. *Al-baligh* means the eloquent one, who through his expression attains the very essence of his inner meaning. *Al-balagh* (كَسَحابِ) means sufficiency, because it reaches the aim. *Bالَغَ mubalaghatan* means he strove and did not fall short. *Tabalaghat bihi al-'illatu* means the illness became severe.

*Al-ghalba'* means a dense, thick garden; among tribes it means a strong, unassailable one. *Al-aghlab* means the lion.

*Laghiba* means he grew weary because of his striving to arrive. *Al-lighab* means the flesh between the teeth. *Al-lagham* (كَكَتِفَ) means corrupt speech; it returns to the sense of exhaustion, and likewise the weak fool. An arrow that was not shot well is called *lughab* (بِالضَّمِّ). *Al-taghallub* means prolonged pursuit.

The mule is among the most robust of animals and the most effective for reaching a destination. *Baghala tabghilan* means he became tired and worn out. Camels walked between an easy amble and a sprint.

Since the object of the message, whose capacity is to arrive, includes good news, He joined to it the warning, using the passive form, because the beneficial element is simply the warning in general, and every person is qualified to be accepted as one who admonishes with it, since whoever hears it is as though he heard it from Allah, for it is distinguished by its inimitability from every other speech. So He said: ﴿and that they may be warned﴾, that is, by whatever warner, so that the proof is established against them, ﴿by it﴾, so that they may fear the punishment of Allah and thereby abandon base things.

Since He had indicated all the branches, both of action and abstention, along with an indication of the root of monotheism, because it is the first step of arrival, He stated it explicitly in its own right, owing to its exalted status, in His saying: ﴿and that they may know that He is﴾, that is, the God, ﴿only one God﴾, so that their aim may be one.

When the indication to the religion, in both root and branches, was complete, He drew attention to the admonitions and parables by reminding them of the signs and created things He possesses, and of the seizing of those nations that opposed Him. He also indicated that the proofs of divine unity and resurrection do not require great reflection, since they are most evident, especially after the warning of the messengers. So He assimilated the *ta'* of the *tafa''ul* form (تاءَ التَّفَعُّلِ), saying: ﴿and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is, among them, ﴿people of pure minds﴾, possessing complete intellects. Thus they open the eyes of their insight, know that there is no arrival for them while heedless, so they keep vigilance and never cease to dwell in the gardens of nearness. And they know, through what is fixed in their natures and what has passed as their customs, that even the least of their rulers would not allow his subjects to act wantonly among themselves without justice, nor repay anyone among them according to what he has earned; for that would be a stripping of him from the rank of rule, which is his distinguishing feature. How then could they claim this of the Most Just of judges? This verse, despite its brevity, has comprised [all the knowledge of the Sharia, in its roots and branches, and the knowledge of the Reality, in its ends and beginnings, in summary form]. The end of the surah has corresponded with its beginning, for this is the very coming out from darkness into light through this Book, which leads to every right course. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the One who grants success in what is right and a good return.
